newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore won't sell SingTel soon.
newsitem.headline: Singapore won't sell SingTel soon.

text.p: Singapore won't sell all, or even most, of its 80 percent stake in telephone monopoly Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) in the foreseeable future, industry sources and analysts said on Wednesday.

Singapore patriarch Lee Kuan Yew was quoted in Singapore media on Tuesday as saying the government should sell its remaining SingTel shares as part of a deregulation process that was needed to keep the city-state ahead of its competitors.
Lee, who was Singapore's prime minister for 31 years until 1990 and whose son Lee Hsien Yang is president and chief executive officer of SingTel, gave no time-frame.
The senior Lee was quoted as saying deregulation should be quick or Singapore would be "wiped out in five to seven years".

Officials at SingTel and state investment company Temasek Holdings, which owns more than 12 billion of the monopoly's 15.24 billion shares on behalf of the government, were unavailable for comment on Lee's views.
But local industry sources said a sale of more than a fairly small part of the government stake would be "inconceivable".
At Singapore $3.10 (US$2.20) per share, the government's current stake in SingTel is worth around S$38 billion, equal to around 15 percent of the whole of the Singapore stockmarket.
Analysts pointed out that the Singapore government had held onto about half the shares in several former state enterprises it now considers fully privatised.
"The government won't sell all its stake," said Winston Lim, telecoms analyst at DBS Securities, a unit of the Development Bank of Singapore Ltd (DBS).
"For example, it holds substantial stakes in DBS (just under 50 percent) and Singapore Airlines (54 percent)".
"The government has said its long-term target is to divest 25 percent of SingTel's shares," he said.
The government placed 100 million SingTel shares with institutions in June and sold 800 million more to 1.5 million Singaporeans in its second public share offer in September.
It has said it will sell a further 300 to 450 million SingTel shares over the next three years.
SingTel is due to lose its monopoly of domestic basic telecommunications services in April 2000 and bits and pieces of its market have been opened up to competition already.

Telecoms companies from the United States, Europe, Hong Kong and Japan have all been reported to be eyeing the Singapore market and could be expected to consider buying into SingTel if it was sold off, analysts said.
But a really large sale of shares would hit SingTel's share price, even if it were spread over several years, analysts said.
Its share price has fallen from S$4.10 in early June, partly due to the sale of some of the new stock.

"A much bigger sale would hit the share price really badly," said a dealer with a local bank. "And it would really skew the Singapore stock market for such a large proportion of the market to be in just one company."

Paul Schymyck, chief Asia-Pacific economist for Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, said the sale of Singapore's stake in SingTel, even over four or five years, would probably be too much for the Singapore market to absorb.
"I am sure the government would not sell the whole lot," Schymyck said. "It might sell a significant chunk -- say 40 percent and retain the rest."
"But Lee is still a major force in Singapore, and if he makes a statement, it is likely to be something the government has in mind...The question is when."
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703199)
